ai-at-work.title: Nvidia is putting its Vera CPUs to work alongside AI agents to speed up chip design
ai-at-work.excerpt: Nvidia Corp. said tonight it’s now running the chip design software its engineers are using to design the next generation of its graphics processing units, on its own silicon. It’s partnering with Cad
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Nvidia is using its own Vera CPUs and AI agents to speed up the chip design process by running EDA software on its own hardware instead of competitors' systems. This matters to digital workplace pros because it shows how companies are increasingly turning internal tools into competitive advantages, which means the software stack your organization relies on could shift quickly if vendors do the same thing. Honestly, it's the tech equivalent of a restaurant buying its own farm, which is smart business but does make you wonder what happens to the companies that were selling them the ingredients.

ai-at-work.title: AWS EC2 compute evolves to meet agentic AI and physical AI demand
ai-at-work.excerpt: Twenty years on, AWS EC2 compute is meeting demand shaped by agentic AI, physical AI, and customers pushing general-purpose cloud infrastructure into new territory its earliest architects never antici
ai-at-work.dwp_take: AWS is upgrading its EC2 compute infrastructure to handle the computational demands of agentic AI and physical AI workloads that are stretching cloud infrastructure in new directions. This matters to digital workplace pros because AI agents increasingly power employee tools, automation, and backend systems that run modern workplace platforms, so compute reliability directly affects user experience. After two decades, EC2 is basically the workhorse that nobody thinks about until it stops working, and now it has to carry even heavier loads without anyone noticing the difference.

ai-at-work.title: Nvidia, other tech giants caution against open-source AI ban in open letter

ai-at-work.dwp_take: Nvidia and other tech firms are publicly pushing back against potential government restrictions on open-source AI models, citing concerns about limiting innovation and competition. For digital workplace professionals, this matters because open-source AI tools are increasingly embedded in productivity platforms, collaboration software, and enterprise workflows that your organizations depend on. Watching tech giants lobby for policy freedom is fine, but someone should probably tell them that most workplace IT departments are still trying to figure out how to govern the open-source AI that's already loose in their systems.

ai-at-work.title: Meta makes Muse Spark 1.1 available to consumers, debuts new Facebook features
ai-at-work.excerpt: Meta Platforms Inc. today made its latest large language model available to consumers through its Meta AI chatbot. The update is rolling out alongside several enhancements to Facebook. Meta’s flagship
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Meta rolled out Muse Spark 1.1 to consumers via its Meta AI chatbot while also adding new features to Facebook, including video-based account verification and a dedicated Marketplace mobile app. This matters because it shows Meta is integrating AI deeper into consumer-facing products, which means workplace communicators need to understand how their employees are using these tools and what that means for corporate messaging on Meta platforms. Honestly, if your company's Facebook strategy doesn't account for AI-generated content and video verification becoming standard, you're already playing catch-up.

digital-culture.title: China-US AI Race Escalates, OpenAI Models Break Free, and Why You Should Check Your Car Alarm
digital-culture.excerpt: On this episode of Uncanny Valley, we dive into accusations that China’s Moonshot AI stole from Anthropic, and how the US Army needs to cut back on AI use.
digital-culture.dwp_take: China's Moonshot AI is accused of lifting tech from Anthropic while the US Army is reconsidering how much it relies on AI systems. This matters because digital workplace leaders are betting billions that AI will transform productivity, and if the foundation is built on stolen IP or unreliable military-grade systems, you're essentially constructing a skyscraper on quicksand. The real takeaway here isn't the geopolitical drama, it's that before you roll out that shiny new AI assistant company-wide, you might want to ask harder questions about where it actually came from and whether it actually works.

industry-news.title: Google Is Spending Even More on AI Than Investors Expected
industry-news.excerpt: Google raised its 2026 capital expenditure forecast to as much as $205 billion as AI demand drives more investment in cloud infrastructure and data centers. The post Google Is Spending Even More on AI
industry-news.dwp_take: Google just told investors it's dropping up to $205 billion on capital spending in 2026, way more than anyone thought, mostly because AI infrastructure is eating money like it's going out of style. This matters because whatever Google builds today becomes the infrastructure your organization will rent tomorrow, which means AI services are about to get cheaper and more powerful whether your company is ready or not. Here's the thing though: companies spending this aggressively on infrastructure usually do it because they're terrified of being left behind, which tells you everything you need to know about where this is actually headed.

industry-news.title: Why Trump Media’s New API Is Raising Questions on Capitol Hill
industry-news.excerpt: Trump Media's planned Truth API is drawing regulatory scrutiny as lawmakers question whether premium access to market-moving Truth Social posts creates fairness concerns. The post Why Trump Media’s Ne
industry-news.dwp_take: Trump Media is launching an API that gives premium subscribers earlier access to posts on Truth Social, which has lawmakers worried about market manipulation and unfair information access. Digital workplace professionals need to pay attention because this touches on real governance questions about data access, API governance, and what happens when social platforms become infrastructure. Here's the thing: if your company's messaging platform had a pay-to-see-first model for market-sensitive information, your compliance team would be having a very bad day, and rightfully so.

industry-news.title: ‘We are now seeing MAI models outperform general-purpose frontier models’: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella touts in-house models to cut spiralling AI costs – and reduce growing reliance on frontier labs
industry-news.excerpt: The Microsoft chief says pricey frontier models don't have to be used for every task, and its own in-house MAI models could be the key to reducing costs.
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft is building smaller, specialized AI models for specific tasks instead of relying on expensive general-purpose models from frontier labs. This matters to digital workplace pros because it signals a shift toward more cost-effective AI deployment, which could finally make generative AI workable for regular organizations instead of just the mega-rich. Nadella's basically saying the emperor's new clothes are too expensive, and maybe we should stop throwing billions at sledgehammers when we actually need a wrench.

industry-news.title: Barracuda expands partner program with new enablement tools
industry-news.excerpt: The cybersecurity vendor has launched new training, demand generation, and partner engagement resources to fuel channel partner growth
industry-news.dwp_take: Barracuda rolled out fresh training materials, demand generation tools, and partner engagement resources to help their channel partners sell more stuff. For digital workplace pros, this matters because better-trained partners mean better security implementations and faster deployments when you actually need vendor support. Look, I've seen enough half-baked partner programs to know that training investments rarely move the needle unless vendors actually enforce competency standards, so I'll believe this one works when I start seeing fewer mediocre implementations in the wild.
